Title: A machine learning-based 18F-FDG PET/CT multi-modality fusion radiomics model to predict Mediastinal-Hilar lymph node metastasis in NSCLC: a multi-centre study
Text:
A machine learning-based 18F-FDG PET/CT
multi-modality fusion radiomics model to
predict Mediastinal-Hilar lymph node metastasis
in NSCLC: a multi-centre study
W. Zhai a,b,d, X. Li a, T. Zhou a,c, Q. Zhou a,b, X. Lin a,b, X. Jiang a, Z. Zhang a,

AIM: To develop and validate a machine learning (ML) model based on positron emission
tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) multi-modality fusion radiomics to improve the
prediction efﬁciency of mediastinal-hilar lymph node metastasis (LNM).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eighty-eight non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with 559
LNs from centre 1 were divided into training and internal validation cohorts (7:3 ratio), and 75
patients with 543 LNs from centre 2 were assigned as external validation cohorts. PET and CT
images were fused by wavelet transform. Multi-modality fusion radiomics features from six im-
ages of lymph nodes were extracted. The multi-modality fusion radiomics (MFR), multi-modality
fusion radiomics þ metabolic parameters (MFRM), CT, PET and PET þ CT models were developed
based on the best one among the 11 ML algorithms. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
curve and the Delong test were used to assess and compare the performance of the models.
RESULTS: The CatBoost algorithm was chosen, and the MFR, MFRM, CT, PET and PET þ CT
models were constructed. The MFR and MFRM models showed a high AUC for predicting LNM
in centre 1 (AUC ¼ 0.950 and 0.952) and centre 2 (AUC ¼ 0.923 and 0.927), and there were
signiﬁcant differences in centre 2 (P¼0.036). The diagnostic efﬁcacy of MFR and MFRM models
was signiﬁcantly higher than CT, PET, PET þ CT models and SUVmax3.5 (P<0.001). The MFRM
prediction was statistically different from the MFR prediction in the hilar/interlobar zone.
CONCLUSION: Both the MFR and MFRM models based on multi-modality fusion radiomics
showed great potential for non-invasively predicting mediastinal-hilar LNM in NSCLC.

Introduction
In patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), an
accurate preoperative assessment of mediastinalehilar
lymph node metastasis (LNM) is crucial for determining the
treatment plan.1 Preoperative invasive LN biopsy and pa-
thology, which may involve mediastinoscopy and endo-
bronchial
ultrasound-guided
transbronchial
needle
aspiration (EBUS-TBNA), are considered the gold standard
methods for assessing the LN status of NSCLC. However, the
practical application of this technique is constrained by its
invasiveness, sampling error, limitation of LNs location and
risk of complications, etc.2e5 18F-FDG PET/CT, which in-
tegrates metabolic and anatomical data of the lesions, is
regarded as a reliable imaging method for detecting LNM in
NSCLC. Nevertheless, the high sensitivity is accompanied by
an intermediate speciﬁcity.6,7
Radiomics represents a high-throughput methodology
for the phenotyping of medical images that can extract and
analyse a variety of quantitative features from images
through the utilisation of computer techniques. It has been
used to predict LNM and prognosis for many malignancies
in different modalities.8e11 Additionally, machine learning
(ML) techniques have been widely used to improve diag-
nostic accuracy.12e14 In recent years, multi-modality fusion
radiomics has received increasing attention.15e17 Multi-
modality fusion radiomics features have not been compre-
hensively investigated, and the potential for diagnostic and
prognostic prediction is substantial. Currently, the investi-
gation of LNM prediction using PET/CT radiomics relies on
the features extracted from independent CT and PET im-
ages. There are no studies that fuse PET and CT images into
one image and extract features for radiomics analysis to
predict LNM. In this study, we attempted to acquire more
meaningful features of LNs from 6 different kinds of images
in NSCLC patients and construct the MFR (multi-modality
fusion
radiomics)
and
MFRM
(multi-modality
fusion
radiomics þ metabolic parameters) models to classify the
mediastinal-hilar LN status of NSCLC patients.
Materials and methods
Patients
The Research Ethics Committee of the Institutional Re-
view Boards of the two centres approved this retrospective
study and waived the informed consent. The medical his-
tories of 3231 patients recently diagnosed with NSCLC who
underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT in two centres from February
2020 to October 2023 were reviewed retrospectively. In-
clusion and exclusion criteria as shown in Fig 1. All LNs
included in the study were histologically proven by EBUS-
TBNA, thoracotomy, ﬁne needle aspiration, excisional bi-
opsy or LN dissection. The locations of the LNs were labelled
and recorded on a map station according to the Interna-
tional Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC)
guidelines. Pathologists then examined the labelled LNs and
reported whether the cancer cells had spread. Patients from
centre 1 were randomly divided into training cohort and
internal validation cohort according to a 7:3 ratio. Patients
from centre 2 were used as the independently external
validation cohort (n¼543). The clinical and pathological
information was obtained from medical records. The
workﬂow of this study is shown in Supplementary Fig 1.
PET/CT acquisition protocol
In centre 1, PET/CT was performed on a Philips Vereos
scanner equipped with digital silicon photomultipliers
(SiPMs). The CT acquisition parameters were 120 kV voltage,
200 mA tube current, and 4 mm slice thickness. PET images
were acquired with 6e8 bed positions at 1.5 min each and
reconstructed using the
3-dimensional
ordered-subsets
expectation maximisation, with a 512  512 matrix and a
voxel size of 4  4  4 mm3. In centre 2, PET/CT was per-
formed on a Siemens Biogragh 64 camera with conventional
photomultiplier tubes. The CT attenuation correction acqui-
sition parameters were 120 kV voltage, 256 mA tube current,
and 3 mm slice thickness. PET images were obtained with
5e7 bed positions at 2 min each and reconstructed using the
TrueX algorithm (2 iterations, 24 subsets), with a 512  512
matrix and a voxel size of 3  3  3 mm3.
In both two centres, all patients fasted for more than 6
hours before the PET/CT scan to ensure the blood glucose
level was below 6.0 mmol/L and 18F-FDG was injected based
on the patient’s weight according to the standard of
0.10e0.15 mCi/kg. The median uptake time in two centres
was 54 min and 60 min, respectively.
PET/CT image processing
After reconstruction, PET images were interpolated to
the CT images and then fused into a single image by
wavelet-based fusion using Matlab R2021b software. The
wavelet coefﬁcients of PET weight were set to 0.2, 0.4, 0.6,
and 0.8 (labelled as WF0.2, WF0.4, WF0.6 and WF0.8) and
the corresponding CT weight was 1 (CT weight). Two nu-
clear medicine physicians who were blinded to the patho-
logic details performed all the metabolic parameters’
measurements via the volumes of interest (VOIs) using
Hermes Hybrid 3D software version 1.0 (Hermes Medical
Solutions), including maximum standardised uptake value
(SUVmax), mean standardised uptake value (SUVmean),
metabolic tumour volume (MTV), and total lesion glycol-
ysis. The VOIs were manually delineated based on the
boundaries of lymph nodes on CT images and then resam-
pled and copied to PET and wavelet fusion (WF) images by
an eight-year-experienced physician and the ﬁnal VOIs
were checked by another senior physician with more than
ten years of experience. Any different opinion was settled by
consensus.
Radiomics features extraction
We utilised the PyRadiomics package version 3.0.1 to
extract the radiomics features from each of the PET, CT,
WF0.2, WF0.4, WF0.6, and WF0.8 images, including ﬁrst-
order features, shape-based 2D and 3D, grey-level co-

occurrence matrix, grey-level dependence matrix, grey-
level run length matrix, grey-level size zone matrix, and
neighbouring grey-tone difference matrix. Advanced ﬁlters
were applied with Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG, sigma 1.0,
2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0mm) and wavelet decompositions (HHH,
HHL, HLH, LHH, LLL, LLH, LHL and HLL). The standardisation
of the feature extraction algorithm was conducted based on
the guidelines proposed by the Image Biomarker Stand-
ardisation Initiative.
Radiomics features selection
We established a three-stage approach within the training
cohort for the selection of features. We ﬁrst randomly
selected 40% of the lymph nodes in the training cohort for
repeated VOI delineation and feature extraction by another
senior physician, then evaluated the stability and reproduc-
ibility of features by calculating ICCs. Features exhibiting ICCs
exceeding 0.8 were considered acceptably reproducible and
selected for further analysis. Next, we conducted the stu-
dents t-test. Features with an adjusted P value below 0.05
were selected and normalised using the z-score. Finally, we
employed
the
least
absolute
shrinkage
and
selection
operator (LASSO) regression method to identify the most
predictive features through 10-fold cross-validation. The
feature that exhibited the lowest cross-validation binomial
deviation was chosen as the ﬁnal feature.
Model training and validation
The
ﬁnal
multi-modality
fusion
radiomics
features
selected by LASSO regression were incorporated into 11 ML
algorithms, including logistic regression, bagging classiﬁer,
KNN, decision tree, random forest, naive Bayes, SVM, GBDT,
XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost, to construct and compare
the models based on the training cohort with 5-fold cross-
validation, and the AUCs of 11 ML models were calculated
(Supplementary File 1). The highest mean AUC of all 5-folds
was selected as the ﬁnal model. Finally, we developed the
MFR (multi-modality fusion radiomics), MFRM (multi-mo-
dality fusion
radiomics þ
metabolic
parameters), CT,
PET and PET þ CT models. The diagnostic performance of all
models and SUVmax3.5 were compared.18e20 We further
assessed the predictive ability of MFR and MFRM in relation
to LNs size at 10 mm threshold. A comparison was also

Statistics analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using R software
version 4.3.2 and MedCalc software version 22.0. Clinical
data that follow a normal distribution is expressed by the
mean  standard deviation. Conversely, data that does not
follow a normal distribution is represented by the median
value along with the interquartile range (IQR). The patient
characteristics of the three cohorts were compared using an
ANOVA test or KruskaleWallis test. The constituent ratio of
counting data was tested using a four-grid table Chi-
squared test or Fisher’s exact test. The receiver operating
characteristic (ROC) curves and decision curves were used
to assess the performance of the models and the DeLong
test was utilised to compare the AUCs of different models. In
addition,
we
used
McNemars
tests
to
verify
the
homogeneity of two ﬁnal models based on LNs location.
Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P<0.05.

The feature extraction and selection
We extracted 7896 multi-modality fusion radiomics
features, 1316 CT features, 1316 PET features and 2632
PET þ CT features as initial features for the multi-modality
fusion radiomics model, CT model, PET, model, and PET þ CT
model, respectively. After comparing the ICCs, there were
3598, 572, 300 and 872 features that remained with higher
than 0.8, indicating good repeatability. After the student’s t-
test, a total of 3390, 454, 286, and 740 features were kept,
respectively. Finally, 28 multi-modality fusion radiomics
features, 17 CT features, 27 PET features and 32 PET þ CT
features were determined by LASSO regression to construct
the ML models (Fig 2, Supplementary Figure 2e5 and
Supplementary File 2).
The ML model selection
We trained the models with 11 common machine
learning algorithms and 28 ﬁnal multi-modality fusion
radiomics features on the training cohort using 5-fold
cross-validation (CV). The mean 5-fold CV AUCs of the lo-
gistic regression, bagging classiﬁer, KNN, decision tree,
random
forest,
Naive
Bayes,
SVM,
GBDT,
XGBoost,
LightGBM and CatBoost models were 0.916, 0.898, 0.744,
0.770, 0.877, 0.937, 0.923, 0.934, 0.894, 0.903 and 0.941,
respectively, and the standard deviation of 5-fold AUC
were 0.016, 0.014, 0.014, 0.019, 0.034, 0.012, 0.014, 0.011,
0.018, 0.011 and 0.009, respectively (Supplementary Fig 6).
Therefore, we chose the CatBoost as our algorithm for
constructing the ﬁnal multi-modality fusion radiomics
model due to its superior mean AUC and lower standard
deviation (0.941  0.009). CT, PET and PET þ CT models
were also established utilising CatBoost algorithm.

Discussion
The precise evaluation of mediastinalehilar LNM before
treatment is important for the development of effective
treatment strategies in NSCLC. Surgery is suggested for
NSCLC with N0-1, whereas neoadjuvant chemotherapy
should be administered preoperatively for NSCLC with N2
LNM, and surgery is not advised for N3 node metastases.22
Therefore, improving the accuracy of detecting LNs is a huge
challenge.
In this multi-cohort study, we innovatively developed
two multi-modality fusion radiomics models to predict
mediastinalehilar LNM. The AUCs of our MFR model were
0.950 and 0.923 in centre 1 and centre 2, respectively. The
combination of MFR and metabolic parameters into MFRM
improved the AUC to 0.952 and 0.927. Both of the MFR and
MFRM exhibit sufﬁciently good diagnostic performance and
a signiﬁcant difference between the performance of the
MFR and MFRM can be observed in centre 2. Studies have
shown that PET/CT has difﬁculty in diagnosing small-sized
lymph nodes.23 We have also conducted predictions on
LNM at 10mm threshold. Our ﬁndings indicate that the MFR
and MFRM models exhibit robust performance in predicting
LNM for both  10 mm and > 10 mm sizes. Our models
exhibit signiﬁcant advantages over traditional CT, PET,

between all models. In our study, the PET þ CT model ex-
hibits superior performance compared with individual PET
and CT models, and the diagnostic effectiveness of the PET
model surpasses that of the CT model in both centre 1 and
centre 2. A study by Qiao et al.24 also reported that the
performance of the PET þ CT model is superior to the
separate PET or CT model in predicting occult lymph node
metastasis (AUCs of the training and internal validation
cohorts were 0.877 and 0.861), while the efﬁciency of the CT
model is higher than that of the PET model (AUCs were
0.839 vs. 0.789, 0.823 vs. 0.736 in two cohorts). One possible
explanation is that all lymph nodes in their study were
SUV<2.5, which represents low uptake of lymph nodes,
may have a potential impact on the extraction of PET fea-
tures related to lymph node metastasis. In terms of the
performance of the multi-modality fusion radiomics model,
our MFR and MFRM model shows a substantial improve-
ment in diagnostic performance when compared with the
PET þ CT model in two centres (Table 2).
With the widespread application of radiomics, several
models based on CT and PET features have been widely
published to improve the diagnostic performance and
speciﬁcity of predicting LNM in NSCLC in the recent years.
Currently, most of the research focuses on the features of
the primary lesion. Cong et al.25 constructed a radiomics-
clinical model based on the enhanced CT features of pri-
mary tumours and showed predictive value for LNM, with
AUCs for training and internal validation of 0.860 and 0.911,
respectively. A study by Zheng et al.26 showed that the
predictive performance of the radiomics model based on
primary tumour was higher than clinical node staging in the
internal validation cohort in NSCLC (AUC ¼ 0.766 vs. 0.685).
Another meeting report stated that the AUC of the PET/CT
radiomics signature derived from the primary tumour
(0.917) was higher than SUVmax (0.806) in predicting
occult lymph node metastasis in the validation cohort.27 An
integrated PET/CT model of primary tumour features and
clinical characteristics developed by Chang et al.28 demon-
strated a higher diagnostic value in predicting LNM of lung
adenocarcinoma (3cm) compared with the single radio-
mics model or clinical model. In addition, there were some
studies based on LN features or the combination of primary
tumour and LN features. In an earlier study, Gao et al.29
reported that a model based on the texture features of LN
and SVM was potential in the diagnosis of mediastinal
lymph nodes (AUC ¼ 0.689). The boosted decision tree
model established based on 40 variables of LN and clinical
information by Yoo et al.13 demonstrated signiﬁcantly
higher accuracy than nuclear medicine physicians for
evaluating LNM in NSCLC (81.0% vs. 76.8%). Ouyang et al.30
integrated PET/CT features of LNs and clinical data into a
combined model to identify mediastinalehilar LNM and
showed a good diagnostic performance among training,
internal validation and validation cohorts (AUC ¼ 0.874,
0.845 and 0.841). Wang et al.2 combined PET/CT radiomic
features from tumours and LNs with clinical features and
reported that it had better predictive efﬁciency in predict-
ing LNM of NSCLC (AUC ¼ 0.93). Rogasch et al.31 developed
an ML model based on routine quantitative parameters of
primary tumour and LNs and clinical information, incor-
porated PET visual scores into the features, and achieved a
high validation AUC of 0.94 (0.89e0.98). Compared with the
above studies, our MFR and MFRM models only rely on the
features of LNs without incorporating primary tumour and
clinical information and have achieved good diagnostic
performance, probably due to the better reﬂection of the
multi-modality fusion radiomics features for the heteroge-
neity of LNM, there is still no relevant report yet. Moreover,
our model achieved speciﬁcity of 0.91 and 0.92, 0.85 and
0.83 in centre 1 and 2, respectively, which is superior to
most previously reported radiomics models and nomo-
grams
(0.500e0.812).13,19,20,32,33

nomogram constructed has been reported to attain a
speciﬁcity of 0.884.24 However, it is important to note that
this result was solely validated in the test set and did not
undergo external validation, with a low sensitivity of 0.654.
It is reported that SUVmax of 3.5 was an indicator of
metastatic LNs in lung cancer.34,35 We compared the
diagnostic efﬁciency of MFR and MFRM models with
SUVmax  3.5. The results indicated that both models
exhibited signiﬁcantly greater AUCs in both centre 1 and
centre 2 as shown in Table 2. The radiomics and MLs
methods were reported to have superior performance
compared with the SUVmax diagnosis in most studies
conducted on mediastinal lymph nodes, and our results
are consistent with them.27,29,36
In the TNM staging system for lung cancer patients, the
clinical and pathologic N descriptor was deﬁned by nodal
status and LN stations that were designated according to
the IASLC lymph node map.37 To assess the predictive per-
formance of our model in different lymph node regions, we
further divided the lymph node prediction results into six
zones. In the supraclavicular zone, the AUC cannot be
calculated because all the LNs are diagnosed as malignant in
two centres. In other zones, the AUCs of MFRM is equivalent
to or higher than that of MFR in centre 1 and centre 2.
Through the McNemars test, we found that the MFRM
predictions were statistically different from the MFR pre-
dictions only in the hilar/interlobar zone when we added
metabolic parameter. In a previous study, SUVmax was
incorporated into seven ML methods to predict LNM, and
the researchers observed that only two ML models exhibi-
ted increased AUC.19 In another study, Wang et al. revealed
that incorporating clinical diagnostic data, such as stand-
ardised uptake value (SUV), into ML methods resulted in
higher AUC values.14 Currently, there is no other research on
the impact of adding metabolic parameters on the diag-
nostic performance of ML models. In our study, the addition
of metabolic parameters has had a limited improvement on
the performance of our model, a possible explanation is the
potential inclusion of metabolic information in multi-
modality fusion radiomics features. The decision curve
also shows that both models have good net beneﬁts.
Therefore, we can consider that MFR and MFRM have
equally excellent predictive performances.
We believe that the utilisation of multi-modality fusion
radiomics features may overcome the shortcomings of in-
dividual PET and CT features, and the setting of different
wavelet coefﬁcients allows us to ﬁnd more responsive fea-
tures of tumour heterogeneity. Our model may be applied to
objectively and non-invasively predict the status of LNM
before treatment based solely on images, thereby increasing
the efﬁciency of LNM diagnosis and supporting the devel-
opment of lung cancer treatment strategies. As introduced
above, numerous studies suggest that the predictive per-
formance of models can be improved by adding primary
tumour
features
and
clinical
information.
Hence,
to
enhance the accuracy of the predictive machine learning
model, our next research aims to further improve the per-
formance of our model by incorporating more primary le-
sions and clinical information.
This research has several limitations. Firstly, there were
more negative LNs than positive LNs in both centre 1 and
centre 2, this may result in a data imbalance. Secondly, in
the data collection stage, we excluded some small-volume
LNs that were unable to extract radiomics features from
the PyRadiomics package due to their insufﬁcient voxels
compared with the resampling sizes. Thirdly, both scanners
were not cross-calibrated that may affect the comparability
of quantitative measurements.
In conclusion, regardless of whether metabolic infor-
mation is added or not, the 18F-FDG PET/CT multi-modality
fusion radiomics model showed good diagnostic perfor-
mance on both photomultiplier tubesand digital PET/CT
systems in predicting mediastinalehilar LNM in NSCLC
patients. For the future, we are planning to explore the
potential of multi-modality fusion radiomics with more
clinical application.
